title: The Cloud and the Three Causes of Storm: How Falsity Is Made Visible and Purified in the Air of the Midst
arc: The teaching opens with the question "What is a cloud?" and then explains that clouds are the mediating state in which trapped archonic powers are made visible against the likeness of the Virgin of Light, working through three causes — cloud-from-fire, cloud-from-water, cloud-from-wind — by which falsity is exposed, struck, captured in tree and flesh, and finally either lifted upward in its first icon or cast down to the seven fossae outside the great sea.
reading:
This chapter answers a deceptively simple question: what is a cloud? The answer turns out to be a complete description of how the cosmic purification operates in the natural mind, using the air of the midst as its arena and the Virgin of Light as its mirror.

A cloud is the mediating state in which moisture (truth in the natural degree) is held in air (perception) and made visible. In the corresponding spiritual operation, the cloud is the place where falsity-from-evil — the archons bound in the elements — is brought up out of its hiding and made manifest in perception, so that judgment can be applied to it. The teaching repeats a fixed structural formula: a cloud rises from below, ascends to the air of the midst, and stands there "against the likeness of the Virgin of Light." The Virgin is the pure receptivity of Divine Wisdom set as a mirror in the middle air; against her uncorrupted likeness, whatever is brought up is seen for what it is. The cloud is therefore a sign — the surviving text repeatedly says "this is the sign" — by which the hidden state of the archons is revealed.

The teaching then distinguishes three causes from which the cloud rises, corresponding to three of the elements of the Living Soul caught in the natural cosmos. The first cloud comes up from the fire: archons of the fire-world are stripped out of the fire, "the sons of fire," and ride up enclosed in this cloud. They are like thieves clothing themselves; the angels stand at their feet and strike them at their appointed hour, knowing they will never do any good. Wherever these fire-archons land — upon a tree, upon cattle, upon men — they burn and destroy in the fire of their body. Here the cloud is the visible sign of corrupt love (fire as lust of self-love) being driven out and judged.

The second cloud is conveyed upward from the water and rises against the Virgin of Light, and its sign is the thunders and lightnings which take shape in the air in sundry likenesses. The archons released from this cloud make frost and hail and snow upon the seed-fruits and crops and produce — that is, they damage in the natural mind precisely those interior truths and works (seeds, fruits) that the Lord is trying to grow there. Even so, this violence is not arbitrary: the very destruction is a "declaring" of what the archons are, a forced confession of falsity made visible in storm.

The third cloud is raised from the wind, again coming up to the air of the midst against the likeness of the Virgin. Its sign is the wind breathed forth in vehemence, the gusts and squalls. The archons of the wind-cloud come down whole "in their icon"; they reach the rivers and the seas and stir up waves within them, waking and overturning the ships and bringing them into wandering. In the correspondence, these are the disordered perceptions (winds) that agitate the natural affections (sea, rivers) and capsize the doctrinal vessels (ships) that carry truth across the natural — every storm at sea is, inwardly, the convulsion of perception in which falsity sets the natural mind reeling.

Set against these three storming clouds is a fourth state which the surviving text describes as the Virgin's own sign: that she is found "gathered in stillness and quietness," and life happens within her in stillness and quietness. This is the contrasting mark — where the archons are released from her in storm, she herself, in her own proper character, is the calm in which life is purified. The same air of the midst that mirrors the violence of the released archons is, in itself, a place of repose; the storms are an alien content briefly held in her stillness so that they may be seen and dealt with.

The second movement of the teaching follows what happens to the archons after the cloud has done its work of exposure. They are captured downward into the begetting of trees and the begetting of flesh — that is, they fall into the generative natural where perception (tree) and body (flesh) are formed — and the angels are stationed as watchers over them. They wait until the hour in which "those archons shall strip themselves of the tree and the flesh and go up to the upper place." There the angels gather them again and pour them out standing on their feet in their first form, in the icons that were within them from the beginning. The light is taken from them — the captive Living Soul is extracted — and the archons themselves, the residue, are cast down to the seven fossae which are outside the great sea, the appointed pits where the fallen abortions fall back to their own midst, stripped of the light that was in them.

Read together, the three causes of storm and the cycle of capture-and-extraction tell one continuous story. The cloud is the cosmic instrument by which the trapped archons of fire, water, and wind are lifted out of their hiding-places, made visible against the icon of the Virgin of Light, struck by the angels, forced down into the generative levels (tree, flesh) where they can be held and watched, and finally compelled to give up the light they had stolen so that the light returns upward in its first icon while the husk is sealed downward into the seven fossae beneath the great sea, at the very feet of the Omophoros who bears the cosmos. Storm and weather, in this teaching, are not mere meteorology; they are the visible face of the great judgment continually at work in the air of the midst, the daily atmospheric form of the cosmic separation of light from darkness.
